description: 1 page, one 11pt paragraph of seven sentences containing (Smith, 2019), (Smith & Jones, 2019, p. 4), (e.g., Lee et al., 2020; Kim, 2021), [12], [3–5] (en dash), the narrative citation "Smith (2019) argues" and the non-citation "(born 1990 in Leeds)".
format: Per page: `lines` = expected buildLines(page).map(l => l.text) in reading order; `spoken` = text to speak with DEFAULT_FILTERS; `spokenReadEverything` = text to speak with READ_EVERYTHING; `skipped` = what DEFAULT_FILTERS drop. Spoken text joins lines with single spaces, de-hyphenates "-" + lowercase line starts, and is normalized (ligatures expanded, soft hyphens removed, NBSP/thin space -> space).
notes: Default (readCitations: false) removes the parenthetical and bracketed citations together with the space before them, and the year from the narrative citation ("Smith (2019) argues" -> "Smith argues").
"(born 1990 in Leeds)" is not a citation and is always spoken.
With readCitations: true (and with READ_EVERYTHING) the text is spoken unchanged: see each page's `spokenWithCitations`.
sentences: Short-term memory fades within seconds without rehearsal (Smith, 2019).
Chunking extends this limit considerably (Smith & Jones, 2019, p. 4).
Several studies replicate the effect (e.g., Lee et al., 2020; Kim, 2021).
Interference, not decay, explains most forgetting [12].
Earlier reviews reached the same conclusion [3–5].
Smith (2019) argues that rehearsal is the key mechanism.
The participant (born 1990 in Leeds) completed every session.
